doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: Hearing an orchestra in the piano; learning Frankie Carle solos
summary: She loved the sound of the piano and learned Frankie Carle's solos note for note at eleven, playing by ear and still struggling to notate harmony.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: What kind of caught your ear when you were young, that led you down this path?
The sound of the piano. Simple as that. I love the sound of the piano. And it’s interesting too because when I hear the sound of the piano I love it, but I also hear a sound of an

orchestra inside the sound of the piano. So I wrote a string quartet, it was very easy for me to play the violin part. It’s like I’m already hearing that. So it’s something I didn’t really notice, but it was there from the beginning, I hear an orchestra there.
I read an interesting little tidbit, that someone said that one of your early influences was Frankie Carle?

Um hmm. Absolutely. Really that was how I learned how to play. I liked his solos. I liked his piano playing. And there was one album, I think it was called “Frankie Carle and his Girlfriends,” and so it was like Diane and Charmaine and Louise and I learned these solos note for note when I was eleven. I played them actually. I began performing them.

The whole solos, the whole thing, exactly what you heard on the record, that’s what I played. So after doing maybe six months of that, and maybe I did eight or ten of them, I knew how to play the piano.
When you were playing them, I’m trying to figure out how to say this, did you know what you were playing from a harmonic standpoint?

I just heard. I still, that’s how I go now, what I do now. People say “What’s that” and, “what’s that,” and I say well it’s the music, here it is, this is what it is. And I still don’t have a definite definition of everything.
Interesting. When you do a lead sheet on a new composition.
You come as close as the chord language will allow?

Well sometimes it’s like a one chord over another chord, but the other chord has maybe it’s over the third of that chord, but you also have to have the tonic, the root of that in there too. So it’s like well you want the E flat but if you called it an E flat that would be on the bottom but it’s not. So then I’ve got three chords there. So there are different ways to notate it by the time I look at that I would never just spontaneously figure it out. So I do what I can.
